title: CS3401 Database Management — Relational Normalization
description: Fundamental normalization levels in relational databases: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF).

style_descriptions.worked_example: Step-by-step table decomposition demonstrating functional dependencies and anomaly elimination
style_descriptions.analogy: Real-world organizational analogies such as filing systems, cataloging, and office hierarchies

quiz.text: What is the primary requirement for a relation to be in First Normal Form (1NF)?

options.a: All non-key attributes depend fully on the primary key
options.b: All attribute values must be atomic (indivisible)
options.d: Every determinant is a candidate key

quiz.text: A student table contains an attribute 'PhoneNumbers' storing a comma-separated list of numbers. Why does this violate 1NF?
When is a table that is already in 1NF guaranteed to be in Second Normal Form (2NF)?

options.a: When the primary key consists of a single attribute
options.b: When all attributes are foreign keys
options.c: When there are no transitive dependencies
options.d: When it has no NULL values

quiz.text: In OrderDetails(OrderID, ProductID, Quantity, ProductName) with PK (OrderID, ProductID), ProductName depends only on ProductID. What anomaly is this?
Which condition violates Third Normal Form (3NF) in a relation that is already in 2NF?

options.a: A non-prime attribute determining another non-prime attribute (transitive dependency)
options.c: A foreign key referencing a primary key
options.d: An attribute having atomic domain values

quiz.text: In Employee(EmpID, DeptID, DeptHead) with PK EmpID, EmpID -> DeptID and DeptID -> DeptHead. How should this be decomposed for 3NF?

options.b: Decompose into Employee(EmpID, DeptID) and Department(DeptID, DeptHead)
options.d: Merge EmpID and DeptHead into composite PK

quiz.text: What is the defining rule of Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)?

options.a: For every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey
options.b: Every non-prime attribute must depend on all candidate keys

quiz.text: Why is BCNF considered strictly stronger than 3NF?

options.a: 3NF allows X -> Y where Y is a prime attribute even if X is not a superkey, but BCNF forbids it
options.b: BCNF eliminates multi-valued dependencies while 3NF does not
options.d: BCNF applies only to single-column keys

first_normal_form.text: A table stores Course(CourseID, Topics) where Topics contains ['Recursion', 'Sorting', 'Trees']. How do we make this 1NF compliant?

options.a: Create a composite key of (CourseID, Topics)
options.b: Flatten so each row contains exactly one atomic topic

second_normal_form.text: Given Enrolls(StudentID, CourseID, Grade, CourseFee) where PK is (StudentID, CourseID) and CourseID -> CourseFee. Why does this violate 2NF?

options.b: CourseFee depends on a proper subset of the composite candidate key

third_normal_form.text: In Customer(CustID, ZipCode, City) where CustID is PK and ZipCode -> City, what type of dependency violates 3NF?

boyce_codd_normal_form.text: If relation R(A, B, C) has functional dependencies AB -> C and C -> B, and candidate keys are AB and AC, why does it violate BCNF?

options.a: In C -> B, C is not a superkey

options.b: A single scalar primitive value per cell

second_normal_form.text: To convert a relation from 1NF to 2NF, what must be removed?

options.b: Partial functional dependencies on composite candidate keys
